chapter: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
title: Freddie Keppard at the Deluxe: his tone, fear of recording and gin
summary: Howard played with Keppard, praising his sweet tone, noting his fear of having his stuff stolen on records, and describing his heavy gin habit.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Sure. Did you play with Cap? Heck yes. Where? At the Deluxe. Oh you did? Sure did. How was he as a trumpet player? Marvelous. Marvelous. Sweet tone and a hell of a lip. Oh yeah? Yes. It's too bad he didn't make any records to my big thing. He had a complex about his records. Somebody wanted to make records they think he wanted to steal his stuff. Yeah. Have you heard that? Yes. Sure. I remember that. It's true. You know one of his sweet numbers was Orly and Rose. I mean he really played it. And then the band picked him up and then swing it you know. Marvelous. I liked him. Was he a nice man? Oh yeah.
Ranked himself to death. Was he very heavy, fast by the time you saw him?

By the time I saw him I didn't know him any other way. Yeah. When he came to Scarborough he was a pretty big guy and he got larger still. Gin. That was a sight to see though. The average person didn't know him, thought he was drinking water. He got a pitcher full of gin. He got these cups that are using the drugs don't they put the cup in? Yeah. He took his picture and set it down. Water, they could see the color of it coming out of the picture. And then when he got to the place where he had a bottle of gin he had them racks, you know, wooden racks, naturally the music's on the rack. He'd pull the bottle up there and pull the rack up, take his drink, see, and then go down at the same time. Sure. Did you ever hear Jimmy Padao? A violin player? Yeah.
